article_title: Dual Language Education and Academic Growth
citation: Angela Johnson. (2020). Dual language education and academic growth. NWEA Research Working Paper. https://www.nwea.org
title: Programs aimed at addressing achievement gaps need to consider summer as well as school-year learning for historically-underserved student populations
description: The article draws a design implication from its seasonal growth findings: "programs aimed at addressing achievement gaps need to consider summer as well as school-year learning for historically-underserved student populations." Because dual language participants showed opposite seasonal patterns in math and reading, interventions targeting achievement gaps must account for both school-year and summer learning rather than school-year growth alone.
requirements: Programs must be evaluated with measures that separate school-year growth from summer learning loss, as the piecewise growth model does.
constraints: The finding comes from one large school district enrolling a substantial English Learner population and one Spanish-English dual language program.
target_learning_goals: Closing achievement gaps with the national average
examples: The study applied a piecewise multilevel growth model to administrative data from a large school district, separating school-year growth from summer loss for dual language participants and nonparticipants.
key_sources: Angela Johnson. (2020). Dual language education and academic growth. NWEA Research Working Paper. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/dual-language-education-and-academic-growth/

article_title: Designing Gateway Statistics and Chemistry Courses for Today’s Students: Case Studies of Postsecondary Course Innovations
citation: Peters, V., Pakhira, D., White, L., Fennelly-Atkinson, R., & Means, B. (2022). Designing gateway statistics and chemistry courses for today's students: Case studies of postsecondary course innovations. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/162
title: Gateway course innovations combine peer-based active learning with a shift from computation toward concepts, reasoning, and application to students' lives
description: Across the case studies, the dominant design pattern pairs peer-based active learning (small groupwork, projects, peer tutoring) with a curricular shift away from computation. The report states that "All five of the five statistics course innovations and two of the three chemistry course innovations involved a shift away from computational approaches toward teaching focused on concepts and reasoning and the application of the discipline to students' lives and future goals." Supporting practices include flipped classrooms, low-stakes formative assessment in place of high-stakes exams, and interactive visualizations or simulations. The report notes these features are congruent with recent National Academies consensus recommendations.
requirements: Instructors willing to restructure class time around individual and peer-based active learning activities
constraints: Structural (department- or institution-level) innovations were less common, and the report notes barriers to departmental or institutional adoption remain
target_learners: first-year undergraduate students in gateway statistics or general chemistry courses, including Black, Latinx, and Indigenous students and students from low-income backgrounds
target_learning_goals: statistical reasoning and application of concepts to real research problems
conceptual understanding and critical thinking in chemistry
examples: Skyline's Data Path course uses a flipped classroom where students watch lecture videos before class and class time supports semester-long projects with SAS coding

The University of Arizona redesigned course engages students through three to seven instructional tasks per lecture asking them to analyze data, model chemical systems, and generate evidence-based arguments

article_title: Seeing Is Solving: MLLMs, Reasoning, and Refusal in Visual Math
citation: Croteau, E., & Heffernan, N. (2026). Seeing Is Solving: MLLMs, Reasoning, and Refusal in Visual Math. https://osf.io/ct7bg/
title: Gate automated scoring and learner-model updates on visual-evidence availability and reliability, treating no-image refusals as missing-context signals
description: For image-dependent math in tutoring systems, the article recommends a reliability-first stance: "gate automated feedback and scoring not on single-run accuracy, but onwithin-model stability and cross-model corroboration". When an item is Required, a system must distinguish learner error from missing-figure conditions before assigning credit or updating mastery; no-image refusals "can be treated as missing-context indicators and used to suppress automated scoring orlearner-model updates until the required visual information is provided". High-agreement items are stronger candidates for automated feedback; low-agreement items should trigger guardrails such as human-authored hints, visual-evidence-binding scaffolds, or deferral.
requirements: The system must log refusal behavior and run stability, and item-level agreement information must be available to set deployment gates
constraints: Applies to image-Required items in intelligent tutoring contexts; the article notes lucky-correct answers without images remain possible and possible training-data exposure is not fully ruled out
target_learners: middle-school mathematics students (Grades 6–8) using intelligent tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: valid automated scoring and learner-model updating on image-dependent math problems
examples: The article recommends that high-agreement items (solved by ≥5 models at majority-correct) are stronger candidates for automated feedback, while low-agreement items should trigger guardrails by design
key_sources: Croteau, E., & Heffernan, N. (2026). Seeing Is Solving: MLLMs, Reasoning, and Refusal in Visual Math. https://osf.io/ct7bg/

article_title: Teaching for Powerful Learning: Lessons from Gateway Public Schools
citation: Cook-Harvey, C. M., Flook, L., Efland, E., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2020). Teaching for powerful learning: Lessons from Gateway Public Schools. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/social-and-emotional-learning-case-study-gateway
title: Gateway's three guiding principles instantiated through a coherent set of schoolwide structures and practices
description: The case study documents how Gateway's founding ideals became three guiding principles—inclusivity and equity, relationships, and continuous improvement—that inform a set of structures and practices. Table 2 lists small schools and class sizes, advisories, an inclusion model, authentic project- and inquiry-based instruction and assessments, scaffolding and differentiation, attention to social-emotional and cognitive development, continuous improvement around an equity agenda, and educator collaboration. The report stresses that "each of the structures and practices works in tandem with the others, so there is a mission-driven coherence schoolwide."
requirements: Schoolwide mission-driven coherence: structures must operate in tandem rather than as isolated programs
constraints: Documented at one charter organization serving about 800 students with small schools and small class sizes
examples: Gateway's advisory system ensures each student has an adult advocate and liaison to the family, and teaching teams share students

article_title: Student Progress before and after California State University's Executive Order 1110
citation: Bracco, K. R., Barrat, V. X., Skjoldhorne, S., & Finkelstein, N. (2021). Student Progress Before and After California State University's Executive Order 1110. WestEd. http://csustudentsuccess.org/multiple-measures
title: Pair entry-level course completion reforms with sustained academic and nonacademic supports, because completing gateway requirements alone does not retain students
description: The report argues that eliminating developmental courses and accelerating first-year GE completion is only a first step: "completion of the A2 and B4 requirements appears to be necessary but not sufficient for long-term retention." It draws on student-success literature and reform examples such as CUNY Start and Georgia State to argue reforms must be intentional and cohesive, support students through their entire college careers, and combine mutually supportive efforts rather than separate initiatives, including advising, tutoring, and financial support.
requirements: Reforms must support students through their entire college careers with mutually supportive efforts rather than separate initiatives, as the report states citing the student-success literature.
constraints: The report states systemwide analyses of academic courses only cannot capture campus-level differences in implementation or the additional supports students receive.
target_learners: First-year CSU students, particularly those placed into supported (Category III/IV) entry-level courses
target_learning_goals: Completion of general education written communication and quantitative reasoning requirements
Retention and progress toward degree completion
examples: The report recommends campus-level analyses examining whether systemwide racial/ethnic differences appear on individual campuses and how supports affect different groups, and suggests campus teams redouble advising for undeclared students.

article_title: Faculty and Student Perspectives on Gateway Math Courses and Courseware
citation: Higgin, T., Holl-Cross, C., Moorjani, A., & Edwards, A., with Cornfield, O., Eisen, S., Hosie, L., McNamara, H., Ray, D., & Tsinnajinnie, B. (2025). Faculty and student perspectives on gateway math courses and courseware. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: User experience design tools for courseware: persona creation kit, journey maps, and ecosystem maps
description: The WestEd team developed freely available user experience design tools grounded in participant data for courseware designers and developers. These include "a modular, deck-based user persona creation kit" with eight student and faculty archetypes plus capacity, challenge, and design thought cards; eight journey maps visualizing a semester-long student experience with friction points and courseware opportunities; and two ecosystem maps illustrating the people, processes, features, and resources that positively or negatively impact success in math courses.
requirements: Cards and maps are rooted in participant data from the study's interviews, surveys, and diary study
constraints: Tools were developed for postsecondary gateway math courseware design contexts
target_learning_goals: Informing courseware design that serves gateway math teaching and learning needs
examples: The persona kit lets designers pair archetypes such as a Reformer faculty member with capacity and challenge cards, then optionally choose two design thought cards to spark design discussion

article_title: Security Education in Higher Education through AI-Powered Gamification
citation: Bingjun Li, Christopher Buzaid, Weihao Qu. (2025). Security Education in Higher Education through AI-Powered Gamification. Journal of Cybersecurity, Digital Forensics and Jurisprudence. https://doi.org/10.65879/3070-5789.2025.01.07
title: Distinction between gamification as a motivation layer and game-based learning as a fully integrated environment
description: The article's background section organizes game-infused education around two approaches: gamification, the application of game design elements such as points, levels, badges, and leaderboards within non-game contexts, and game-based learning (GBL), which employs complete games or interactive simulations as the primary medium of instruction. The article states that "gamification serves as a motivation layer over conventional contexts, while GBL constitutes a fully integrated learning environment," attributing this recent clarification to Caponetto et al. and related reviews. It positions its own games closer to GBL-style immersive simulation enriched with AI adaptivity.
requirements: Designers must decide which approach fits: enriching existing instruction with motivational elements versus transforming the activity itself into a game
constraints: The article notes early research often blurred the distinction between the two concepts, and the framing is attributed to prior literature rather than tested here
target_learners: instructional designers choosing between gamification and GBL
target_learning_goals: engagement and motivation in security education
experiential learning in authentic interactive environments
examples: The article classifies traditional platforms like Mimecast as passive instruction, gamified micro-games as interactive enrichment, and the Sentinel phone-scam simulator as immersive experiential learning

article_title: Development and validation of the generative AI assessment literacy scale for higher education students
citation: Nie J, Zhang Z, Lu X, Zhang Y and Zhang M (2026) Development and validation of the generative AI assessment literacy scale for higher education students: psychometric evidence and associations with feedback engagement and academic integrity. Front. Educ. 11:1934632. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1934632
title: Generative AI Assessment Literacy Scale (GAA-LS), an 18-item five-dimension instrument
description: The GAA-LS is a self-report questionnaire measuring higher education students' assessment-specific capacity to use GenAI responsibly. The final version includes 18 items across five dimensions: assessment criteria awareness (4 items), AI-task appropriateness judgment (4 items), verification and evidence checking (4 items), ethical attribution and academic integrity (3 items), and feedback uptake and revision literacy (3 items). Items use a five-point Likert scale, and subscale and total scores are computed as mean scores, "with higher scores indicating stronger perceived capacity to use GenAI responsibly in assessment-related tasks."
requirements: Respondents need awareness of or experience with GenAI tools and experience with course assignments or assessment tasks, per the study's inclusion criteria.
constraints: The sample was limited to one national higher education context and was not designed to be nationally representative; the authors state the scale may require adaptation for secondary education, professional training, or international contexts.
target_learning_goals: diagnosing students' assessment-specific GenAI literacy to inform targeted teaching and institutional policy evaluation
examples: Sample items include "I can judge whether AI-generated content meets the assessment criteria of a course task" and "I verify the accuracy of information, references, and reasoning provided by GenAI before using them in assessed work."

article_title: A Guiding Framework for K-12 Teachers in Creating AI-powered Learning Technologies through Vibe Coding
citation: Song, Y., Choi, S., Kim, J., Kim, Y., Weisberg, L., & Moon, J. (2026). A Guiding Framework for K-12 Teachers in Creating AI-powered Learning Technologies through Vibe Coding. https://x.com/karpathy/status/1886192184808149383
title: GAIDE: A Guiding Framework for AI-Integrated Design for Educators
description: GAIDE is a framework supporting K-12 teachers in creating AI-powered learning technologies through vibe coding. It combines Design Thinking phases with adapted INTERACT design components, bookended by an initial Understand AI phase and a final Reflect on Ethical Application phase. Revisions from the empirical workshop included that "Learning Environment was removed, and Learning Objectives was newly introduced" in the Design phase, and the framework visualizes a non-linear, iterative cycle of collaborative design.
requirements: Foundational understanding of AI established before the design and development process begins
Mentor support during prototyping and testing phases
constraints: Derived from one eight-week workshop with three teachers; the authors state more user cases are needed
examples: In the workshop, teachers used Google AI Studio to prototype Math Mysteries, guided through INTERACT design components such as Learning Objectives, Learner Differentiation, and Knowledge Mapping

article_title: Development and applications of Generative AI in architectural design studios
citation: Leman Figen Gül, Burak Delikanlı, Oğulcan Üneşi, Ertuğrul Ömer Gül. (2025). Development and applications of Generative AI in architectural design studios. ITU A|Z • Vol 22 No 3 • November 2025 • 751-774. https://doi.org/10.58278/0.2025.109
title: GAI-A (Generative Artificial Intelligence in Architecture) interface with Collage Tool
description: GAI-A is a user-friendly GenAI interface for architectural design developed for non-programmers, built with React.js frontend and Flask backend. The article states: "Our system operates through a sequential pipeline of established technologies, employing both image-to-prompt and prompt-to-image creation (at Midjourney v5.2) alongside a LLM to generate an output image from an input collage (Figure 3)." Users create collages in a GUI; the backend generates prompts describing the collage, refines them via ChatGPT, and produces a final 'render' image. Its purpose is to transform image collages into cohesive singular representations of the user's intended theme.
requirements: An easily navigable interface that streamlines collage-making aligned with students' individual styles and image preferences, as expressed by students
constraints: Model parameters were incorporated informed by student feedback; specialized Stable Diffusion models and workflows were added in subsequent versions
examples: Workshop VII tested the Collage Tool, where students created architectural collages merging conceptual visuals from their projects

article_title: When AI Wears Many Hats: The Role of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Marketing Education
citation: Narang, Unnati, Vishal Sachdev, and Ruichun Liu. (2025). When AI Wears Many Hats: The Role of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Marketing Education. Journal of Public Policy & Marketing. https://doi.org/10.1177/07439156251328237
title: GAI role framework: tutor, teammate, and tool mapped onto teaching, social, and cognitive presence
description: The article integrates Role Theory with the Community of Inquiry (CoI) model to propose that GAI can assume three roles in marketing education. As a tutor, GAI provides personalized instruction and helps with learning specific concepts and skills; as a teammate, it collaborates by sharing ideas and offering different perspectives; as a tool, it completes assigned tasks efficiently. Each role is posited to influence teaching, social, and cognitive presence differently, shaping learning experience and workplace readiness.
requirements: Learning objectives of the marketing course determine which role GAI should assume
Instructors provide instructions (system prompts) to the GAI chatbot for each role
constraints: The roles often overlap and interact dynamically in practice, particularly in online and hybrid formats
Framework validated only on a convenience sample and should be expanded in future research
examples: In Principles of Marketing, GAI offers personalized feedback on student projects; in Marketing Research, GAI facilitates brainstorming sessions; in Marketing Analytics, GAI helps apply data analytics techniques and generates code and reports
key_sources: Narang, Unnati, Vishal Sachdev, and Ruichun Liu. (2025). When AI Wears Many Hats: The Role of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Marketing Education. Journal of Public Policy & Marketing. https://doi.org/10.1177/07439156251328237

title: Multipronged exploratory study: syllabi review of 11 marketing courses plus survey of 14 faculty and interviews
description: The article's empirical base is a multipronged exploratory analysis combining a review of marketing course syllabi, a survey of marketing educators, and follow-up qualitative interviews. The review "covered 11 distinct marketing courses taught by the marketing faculty at a large midwestern U.S. public university," followed by "a survey of 14 full-time faculty members" who teach these courses. It extracted learning objectives and topics from syllabi and mapped instructors' reported GAI use to course type and objectives.
requirements: Course syllabi with stated learning objectives
Instructor participation in the survey and follow-up discussions
constraints: The sample of courses and instructors was chosen as a convenience sample for providing preliminary validation of the framework and should be expanded in future research
target_learning_goals: aligning GAI use with course learning objectives
examples: Table 4 illustrates how GAI is used in Marketing Research (data analysis and visualization), New Product Development (project-based learning and ideation), Digital Marketing (content generation), and Marketing Analytics (data analysis, chatbot, discussion forums)

article_title: When AI Wears Many Hats: The Role of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Marketing Education
citation: Narang, Unnati, Vishal Sachdev, and Ruichun Liu. (2025). When AI Wears Many Hats: The Role of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Marketing Education. Journal of Public Policy & Marketing. https://doi.org/10.1177/07439156251328237
title: One assignment, three GAI role implementations: tutor, teammate, and tool modifications
description: The article presents a reusable assignment design pattern in which a single marketing assignment is modified for each GAI role. In a social media marketing assignment on viral campaigns, the tutor version uses a Socratic dialogue with GAI as an expert guide, the teammate version has students collaborate with GAI while maintaining a critical approach, and the tool version restricts GAI to data gathering and analysis while requiring independent recommendations. The pattern advances specific learning objectives within the role framework.
requirements: Instructors provide explicit instructions (system prompts) to the GAI chatbot for each role
Assignment instructions specify appropriate use cases for GAI
constraints: The tool implementation requires that final analysis and recommendations be independently formulated by students
examples: Students identify three viral marketing campaigns, then use GAI as a tutor to evaluate each campaign, respond to its guiding questions on social transmission and emotional resonance, or use it to compile engagement statistics while formulating their own recommendations

article_title: GenAI Use and GenAI-Assisted Learning Procrastination in University Students: The Roles of Planned Behavior Constructs and Learning GenAI Anxiety
citation: Li Zilin, Huang Jiali, Cui Zhaodi. (2026). GenAI Use and GenAI-Assisted Learning Procrastination in University Students: The Roles of Planned Behavior Constructs and Learning GenAI Anxiety. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071256
title: GenAI-assisted learning procrastination as a TPB-based intention–behavior gap construct distinct from deliberate non-use
description: The article extends the Theory of Planned Behavior to GenAI-assisted learning by defining GenAI-assisted learning procrastination (GALP) as "the unnecessary delay in initiating or completing the use of GenAI to support learning tasks, despite holding a genuine intention to use the technology". Within this framework, attitude, subjective norm, and perceived behavioral control shape intention, which relates to procrastination, while learning GenAI anxiety acts as a boundary condition on the intention–procrastination link. The authors explicitly position this as "a contextual extension of TPB rather than a fundamental theoretical breakthrough".
requirements: The focal behavior must be clearly specified so that attitude, norm, control, intention, and outcome refer to the same target behavior, as the article states.
constraints: The framework is offered as initial empirical evidence from a cross-sectional design; findings are conditional associations rather than causal evidence, and generalizability requires further investigation.
target_learning_goals: timely completion of GenAI-assisted learning tasks such as daily assignments, final-term assignments, and examination preparation
examples: The study operationalized all TPB constructs with self-developed scales referencing the focal behavior of GenAI-assisted learning task completion and tested the model with path analysis among 1243 Chinese university students.

article_title: The effects of generative AI on collaborative problem-solving and team creativity performance in digital story creation: an experimental study
citation: Wei, X., Wang, L., Lee, L.-K., & Liu, R. (2025). The effects of generative AI on collaborative problem-solving and team creativity performance in digital story creation: an experimental study. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 22:23. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-025-00526-0
title: GAI-assisted DST creation pattern integrating problem-based learning across four DST stages and six projects
description: A 20-week curriculum pattern that structures collaborative digital story creation around Robin and Pierson's (2005) four DST stages: "(1) define, collect, and decide; (2) select, import, and create; (3) decide, write, record and finalize; and (4) demonstrate, evaluate, and replicate." These stages were instantiated as six projects (story scenario, storyboard, static images, animation, editing/finalization, sharing/publishing), each embedding a problem-based learning procedure (identify goal, gather information, define problem, generate solutions, evaluate solutions, make a decision). Teams of five students completed CPS tasks within each project, with the experimental group supported by ChatGPT, Midjourney, Runway, and CapCut.
requirements: Teams of five students working collaboratively on sequenced DST projects
A curriculum organized by instructors with multidisciplinary expertise (DST design, GAI tools, educational technology)
constraints: Studied over a 20-week program with 120-minute weekly sessions in a higher education setting
target_learners: university students majoring in Educational Technology
examples: The experimental group produced six DST videos (2 min 52 s to 5 min 6 s) on themes such as "Why do bears have short tails?" and "The wizard's new pet" using GAI tools at each stage

article_title: Gap Analysis: An Innovative Look at Gateway Courses and Student Retention
citation: Bloemer, W., Day, S., & Swan, K. (2017). Gap analysis: An innovative look at gateway courses and student retention. Online Learning, 21(3), 5-14. https://doi.org/10.24059/olj.v21i3.1233
title: Gateway-course effects are mediated by student type and academic stage rather than uniform across students
description: The article's organizing account is that course effectiveness must be judged in context: students enter "with widely different backgrounds and learning goals" and "change significantly over the course of their studies." It operationalizes this by classifying students into four Student Types (Native Freshmen, Honors Freshmen, On-ground Transfers, Online Transfers) and five life-cycle stages (First Term, Second Term, Second Year, Third Year, Later), and predicting outcomes from these plus prior GPA and DFW fraction. The authors state the results "plainly suggest that the effects of gateway courses are mediated by student types and academic stages."
requirements: Classification of students by entry type (freshman vs transfer, honors, online vs on-ground) and academic life-cycle stage
Course-level grade and persistence records tied to short-term enrollment measures
constraints: Results are clearly limited to the undergraduate population at the university studied
examples: The four-year institutional dataset at a small Midwestern public university was analyzed with binary logistic regression predicting DFW probability per course
key_sources: Bloemer, W., Day, S., & Swan, K. (2017). Gap analysis: An innovative look at gateway courses and student retention. Online Learning, 21(3), 5-14. https://doi.org/10.24059/olj.v21i3.1233

article_title: Gap Analysis: An Innovative Look at Gateway Courses and Student Retention
citation: Bloemer, W., Day, S., & Swan, K. (2017). Gap analysis: An innovative look at gateway courses and student retention. Online Learning, 21(3), 5-14. https://doi.org/10.24059/olj.v21i3.1233
title: Gap-analysis method for identifying gateway courses via predicted versus observed DFW rates and persistence gaps
description: A learning-analytics method using institutional student records. A binary logistic regression predicts the probability a student posts a D, F, or W grade using Student Type, life-cycle stage, prior cumulative GPA, and prior DFW fraction; predicted and observed rates are recorded per course and "the difference (Gap) between them calculated." A second gap compares persistence of students in a course to students in all courses of the same type at the same degree-path point, by student type and stage.
requirements: Multi-year institutional records of end-of-term grades and next-term enrollment or graduation
Student classification into types and life-cycle stages
Predictive model including prior GPA and prior fraction of DFW grades, which "is known to add predictive power over prior GPA alone"
constraints: DFW rates use end-of-term grades rather than final transcript grades
Persistence is measured as enrollment in the next regularly scheduled term or graduation
examples: Applied to 34 general education courses at a small Midwestern public university over four years

article_title: Guidelines for the Design and Implementation of Game Telemetry for Serious Games Analytics
citation: Gregory K.W.K. Chung. (2015). Guidelines for the Design and Implementation of Game Telemetry for Serious Games Analytics. In C.S. Loh et al. (eds.), Serious Games Analytics. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-05834-4_3
title: Game telemetry as systematic behavioral observation linking player events to inferences about learning
description: The chapter conceives game telemetry as "the data associated with specific game events, the state of a game, or other parameters of interest," captured to a permanent external store using a predefined record format rather than ad hoc logging. It flows from the behavioral observation tradition, where the two most important properties are "the precise deﬁnition of the behavior to observe" and "the connection between the behavior and a theoretical framework within which the behavior is interpreted." Telemetry is the first element in the chain of reasoning from behavior to inferences about learning.
requirements: The set of behavioral acts of interest must be well defined prior to observation
A clear definition, specified a priori, of what to observe and how to code it, a structured sampling method, a reliable recording method, and reliability and validity evidence of the coding scheme
constraints: The approach focuses solely on supporting measurement of performance of play-learners in serious games, not entertainment or monetization
target_learners: play-learners in serious games, e.g., underprepared students learning fractions
target_learning_goals: inferences about players' learning and performance during gameplay
examples: The telemetry system in Save Patch was based on these guidelines, with behavior defined in terms of the cognitive demands of successful gameplay

article_title: Game Jams as Valuable Tools for the Development of 21st-Century Skills
citation: Contreras-Espinosa, R.S.; Eguia-Gomez, J.L. (2022). Game Jams as Valuable Tools for the Development of 21st-Century Skills. Sustainability 2022, 14, 2246. https://doi.org/10.3390/su14042246
title: Run game jams as voluntary extracurricular additions to courses rather than core formal-course components
description: The article recommends organizing game jams outside mandatory formal coursework, because voluntariness and novelty sustain motivation. The authors state the idea of introducing game jams in formal school contexts "should be seen as an addition, instead of a core component", warning that mandatory use and repetitive per-subject jams could lose positive learning outcomes.
requirements: Participation should be voluntary to protect motivation
Teachers or tutors need the necessary competencies for game-jam pedagogy
constraints: In public schools in Mexico each subject is taught by a different teacher, so per-subject jams would become repetitive
Formal-course integration depends on the characteristics of each course
target_learning_goals: 21st-century skills: critical thinking, creativity, communication, collaboration
examples: The three studied jams were voluntary events for students of a Mexico City family-development program, organized as additional activities rather than within formal courses

title: Game jams as pedagogical spaces combining co-creation, co-production and co-design with four learning types
description: The article frames game jams as constructivist learning environments that emulate industrial processes (co-creation, co-production, co-design) and host four learning types: "The type of learning that takes place during game jams is not very different from that from typical educational environments and includes (1) cooperative, (2) project-based, (3) problem-based, and (4) collaborative learning." Through these processes the events are said to contribute to 4C skill development.
requirements: A tutor able to promote beneficial interaction, which is crucial for collaborative learning to succeed
constraints: In such a short collaborative event it is unrealistic to expect participants to acquire all skills or learn to program
target_learners: adolescent students (12–16) in informal and extracurricular settings
examples: The studied jams combined cooperative task division, tutor-supported project work, problem-solving during testing, and collaborative creation of a shared game

title: Game jam resource kit: non-digital and digital materials, software, venue and devices for 4C-focused jams
description: A concrete set of materials, tools and venue conditions the article identifies as necessary to organize a game jam aimed at 4C skill development. Laptops with event software installed, plus extra devices in case participants' laptops fail
Tutors and voluntary workers to support idea generation, materials and technical problems
constraints: Even paper-based teams should have computer and Internet access to check game mechanics and the event theme

examples: In the studied events, one workgroup developed concepts and dynamics through paper models, while most games were created with GameMaker Studio, Adobe Photoshop, and Scratch

article_title: Zoo U: A Stealth Approach to Social Skills Assessment in Schools
citation: Melissa E. DeRosier, Ashley B. Craig, and Rebecca P. Sanchez. (2012). Zoo U: A Stealth Approach to Social Skills Assessment in Schools. Advances in Human-Computer Interaction. https://doi.org/10.1155/2012/654791
title: Combine detailed game logs of socially relevant behavior with external skill measures to incrementally improve embedded assessment accuracy
description: When building an embedded (stealth) assessment, developers should log socially relevant player behavior in detail and analyze it against independent external measures of the same skill, using mismatches to revise items and scoring. The article reports that "detailed game logs of socially relevant player behavior combined with external measures of player social skills provided an eﬃcient vector to incrementally improve the accuracy of the embedded assessments." In Zoo U this meant refining dialogue choices that did not relate in expected directions with teacher ratings.
requirements: Minute annotated logging of the times and locations of every player click event
External measures of the target skill (e.g., teacher ratings) collected for the same students
constraints: The optimal thresholds for behavioral indicators were not evident at initial design and had to be established empirically from gameplay logs
target_learning_goals: accurate embedded assessment of social skills
examples: Log data from the first iterative test were used to refine dialogue choices that did not relate in the expected directions with teacher ratings of students' social skills

article_title: CHAPTER 8 ‒ Assessing Persistence in Educational Games
citation: Ventura, M., Shute, V., & Small, M. (2013). Assessing Persistence in Educational Games. Design Recommendations for Intelligent Tutoring Systems - Volume 2: Adaptive Instructional Management. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Assessing+Persistence+in+Educational+Games
title: Game-based assessment of persistence (GAP): time spent on unsolved problems
description: The GAP is a log-derived, performance-based measure of persistence. As the authors define it, "we developed a game -based assessment of persistence (GAP), which is derived from time spent on unsolved problems over all events in the player's log file over the five sessions." Time on unsolved problems is summed across all repeated attempts and averaged across unsolved problems out of a possible 74; time on solved problems is excluded because solution times primarily reflect skill. Longer times on difficult problems are taken to indicate greater persistence.
requirements: Requires log files recording time spent per problem visit across sessions; longer times spent on difficult problems should indicate greater persistence
constraints: Time on solved problems is not an indicator of persistence because solution times are primarily based on skill
examples: Validation used impossible anagrams and picture comparison tasks where the score is time spent on impossible trials

article_title: Examining the Use of Game-Based Assessments for Hiring Autistic Job Seekers
citation: Willis, Colin, Tracy Powell-Rudy, Kelsie Colley, and Joshua Prasad. 2021. Examining the Use of Game-Based Assessments for Hiring Autistic Job Seekers. Journal of Intelligence 9: 53. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence9040053
title: Game-based assessment packages (Disconumbers, Shapedance, Digitspan) measuring non-social cognitive ability
description: The study used two packages of serious games measuring cognitive ability: Disconumbers, a "memory and math-based game"; Shapedance, a "visuospatial ability task similar to the Mental Rotation task"; and Digitspan, a memorization game similar to the digit span task on the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale. Scores range from zero to five, are true interval scores, and games progress through timed levels with increasing challenge. Each game is a serious game intended not to entertain but to make a functional task more engaging.
requirements: Games are combined into packages of two games taken in sequence as part of a longer hiring assessment
constraints: The games measured cognitive traits selected because they are least likely to differentiate autistic and neurotypical individuals; findings do not generalize to other cognitive abilities or content such as emotional intelligence or personality
target_learners: college-graduate job seekers, including autistic job seekers
target_learning_goals: assessment of non-social cognitive ability (working memory, visuospatial ability, math-based memory) for hiring selection
examples: 263 autistic and 323 general-population candidates completed one of the two packages as part of a real-world hiring assessment

article_title: Auditory attention in childhood and adolescence: An event-related potential study of spatial selective attention to one of two simultaneous stories
citation: Karns Christina M., Isbell Elif, Giuliano Ryan J., Neville Helen J. (2015). Auditory attention in childhood and adolescence: An event-related potential study of spatial selective attention to one of two simultaneous stories. Developmental cognitive neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2015.03.001
title: Gain-control account of auditory selective attention across development, with later endogenous attention processes
description: The article advances the account that spatial selective attention operates by modulating the amplitude of maturing auditory early-latency evoked potentials — a gain-control mechanism — and/or by invoking later, potentially endogenous attention processes. Support is the difference-wave analysis showing "a multiphasic morphology that was similar to the attend and unattend waveforms for each age group", taken as "evidence for gain-control modulation". The authors state the evidence "is mixed and seems to depend on probe type": gain control fits nonlinguistic probes, while linguistic probes show sustained later modulation suggesting additional endogenous processing.
requirements: Interpretation requires tracking maturational changes in the underlying auditory evoked potentials, since attention modulation interacts with developing morphology and latency
constraints: The difference-wave morphology does not rule out other mechanisms operating with coincidentally similar morphology and topography
Evidence for gain control is mixed and depends on probe type; a pure gain-control account would predict N1 modulation that was not observed
target_learning_goals: auditory spatial selective attention in acoustically noisy, competing-speech environments
examples: Difference-wave time-bin analyses found significant attention effects corresponding with measured P1-N1-P2 peaks, plus prolonged effects at 300–500 ms for linguistic probes across all age groups

article_title: Promoting regulation of equal participation in online collaboration by combining a group awareness tool and adaptive prompts. But does it even matter?
citation: Strauß, S., & Rummel, N. (2021). Promoting regulation of equal participation in online collaboration by combining a group awareness tool and adaptive prompts. But does it even matter? International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (2021) 16:67–104. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09340-y
title: Group awareness tool with gini-triggered adaptive prompts implemented as Moodle plugins
description: The collaboration support was implemented as Moodle plugins controlled by an automated support system and always visible in the sidebar of the main page, group wiki, and group forum. The GAT visualized participation as bar graphs of words each member contributed to the group's wiki and forum, with a legend identifying members; the adaptive prompt, shown in a box above the GAT, suggested a shared-regulation action plus a motivating statement. Per the article, "If the gini coefficient was equal to 0.5 or greater, a prompt was displayed", drawn from a pool of six synonymous prompts.
requirements: An automated support system that updates counts; the article notes "The support was automatically updated whenever a student had contributed to the group’s wiki or forum".
constraints: Prompts were displayed only when the gini coefficient reached 0.5 or greater; below that threshold the system "informed the group that there are currently no new suggestions available".
The first prompt appeared three days after the task started, to reduce redundant prompts from the first group member opening the conversation.
target_learners: University undergraduate students in an online course working in groups of four
target_learning_goals: Regulating the distribution of participation during online collaboration
examples: The bar-graph GAT displayed word counts per member in the group wiki, forum, or total, with toggling checkboxes, online status, and message shortcuts.

title: Wiki learning environment with knowledge bars and participation bars at individual, group, and subgroup levels
description: A self-designed wiki environment on energy sources in which awareness information appears as horizontal bars in the discussion forum in the header and next to threads. Yellow knowledge bars visualize subgroup knowledge; blue participation bars visualize contribution counts, with low, medium, and high levels presented at individual, whole-group, and subgroup levels across 12 discussion threads on energy types.

constraints: The wiki article itself contained no GA visualizations; bars appeared only in the discussion forum header and beside threads.

article_title: Group awareness and regulation in computer-supported collaborative learning
citation: Lenka Schnaubert, Daniel Bodemer. (2022). Group awareness and regulation in computer-supported collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09361-1
title: GA participates in three regulatory cycles: regulating GA, regulating social interaction, and regulating partner schema building
description: The article models GA as an integral part of three regulatory processes during CSCL, illustrated in Fig. 2 as "Three types of regulation: (1) regulating GA, (2) regulating social interaction, (3) regulating partner schema building". In cycle (1) learners metacognitively monitor and control their own partner-related cognitions against task- and situation-appropriate standards. In cycle (2) GA guides how learners act, react, and adapt interaction based on perceived social conditions. In cycle (3) GA serves as the informational basis for refining and correcting partner models stored in long-term memory.
requirements: coherent, relevant GA requires continuous regulation and cannot rely on automatic perception
task demands, technological setup, and availability of social information shape which regulatory processes are possible
constraints: the framework focuses on individual self-regulation of cognition and behavior directed at the social context, explicitly not covering self-, co- and shared regulation of content learning itself
some cited awareness tools are static and not suitable to support the full regulatory cycle
target_learning_goals: social interaction regulation, partner modelling, and self-regulation of group-directed cognition
examples: When learners notice a misalignment in understanding of a key concept, they may discuss it to resolve the conflict, then terminate resolution and move on
key_sources: Lenka Schnaubert, Daniel Bodemer. (2022). Group awareness and regulation in computer-supported collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09361-1

article_title: Group awareness and regulation in computer-supported collaborative learning
citation: Lenka Schnaubert, Daniel Bodemer. (2022). Group awareness and regulation in computer-supported collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09361-1
title: Use GA tools to provide information that guides learning decisions, but design them as supports for, not replacements of, metacognitive regulation
description: GA tools aim at fostering collaborative learning by providing information necessary to make adequate learning decisions, and they process learner data in ways that may exceed human information-collection capabilities. However, because GA is a psychological construct requiring conscious regulation, the article states that "while GA tools may assist by providing information about learning partners, they do not replace the metacognitive regulation processes involved". Tool-based design should therefore be grounded in a conceptual understanding of GA itself.
requirements: designers need a conceptual understanding of GA before tool-based research can explain collaborative processes or design effective tools
constraints: efforts toward attaining GA are secondary to knowledge construction and may even be harmful to learning under certain circumstances due to collaboration load
static awareness tools not intended to catch the dynamics of collaboration cannot support the full regulatory cycle
target_learners: collaborative learners supported by CSCL environments
target_learning_goals: adequate learning decisions and collaboration based on computer-provided group information
examples: GA tools have continuously been shown to be of great value for supporting CSCL and have been linked to partner modelling accuracy, learning processes, and learning success in prior tool studies cited by the article

A dedicated reflection phase about which groups write concrete plans for the next collaboration
constraints: Applied after the first collaboration phase only, targeting past interaction rather than live interaction

article_title: Graphical means for inspecting qualitative models of system behaviour
citation: Anders Bouwer, Bert Bredeweg. (2010). Graphical means for inspecting qualitative models of system behaviour. Instr Sci 38:173–208. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9083-4
title: GARP framework for qualitative reasoning and modelling: model fragments and scenarios simulated into state–transition graphs
description: GARP is a framework for qualitative reasoning and modelling in which "Given a scenario (a description of a particular situation) and a library of model fragments (the generic domain knowledge) as input, the simulation engine produces a state–transition graph as output". Model fragments come in categories (description views, assumptions, process and agent fragments, composition views), each with conditions and consequences; the engine recursively applies applicable fragments to infer states and transitions, including branches when outcomes are underdetermined. Input and output are in predicate logic (Prolog) format, which the article notes is challenging for humans to read.
requirements: A scenario describing system structure and initial quantity values
a library of model fragments encoding generic domain knowledge
constraints: The predicate logic format is challenging for humans to read and makes overview difficult for novices, motivating VISIGARP
target_learners: future decision makers in sustainable development
target_learning_goals: explaining and predicting system behaviour qualitatively
examples: The Cerrado domain library contains 79 model fragments covering processes such as natality, mortality, immigration, emigration and interaction effects like predator–prey and amensalism

citation: Ratinho, E., Figueiredo, M., Estêvão, D., Faísca, L., & Martins, C. (2026). Gamification on Mathematics Engagement and Motivation in Secondary School and Higher Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10108-1
title: Table 4 mapping of gamification elements to learner motivational characteristics
description: The review provides a synthesis table (Table 4) mapping eight game elements — avatar, badges, progress/levels, ranking/leaderboards, collaborative rankings/team tasks, score/points, timer/time pressure, and rewards — to the learner profiles for which each is "Possibly effective" and "Possibly less effective", with example studies. For instance, badges suit learners low in intrinsic motivation but may be perceived as controlling by learners initially high in intrinsic motivation; leaderboards suit learners high in extrinsic motivation but may reduce autonomy and competence for learners high in intrinsic motivation.
requirements: Matching elements to learners' motivational profiles requires knowledge of learner characteristics; the review points to player typologies such as the HEXAD model as validated tools to identify motivational preferences
constraints: The table's entries are qualified as "possibly" effective or less effective, drawn from the included studies rather than tested as moderator hypotheses

target_learning_goals: Tailoring gamification elements to learner motivation and engagement needs

article_title: Connecting Sociocultural Theory and Educational Practice: Galperin's Approach
citation: Arievitch, I.M., & Haenen, J.P.P. (2005). Connecting Sociocultural Theory and Educational Practice: Galperin's Approach. Educational Psychologist, 40(3), 155-165. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15326985ep4003_2
title: Galperin's spiral model of stepwise formation of mental actions
description: The article presents Galperin's teaching strategy as a spiral model in which learning proceeds through alternating levels of acting while the quality of the action improves. The authors state that "the stepwise process of the formation of actions can be most adequately represented by a spiral model," with five levels per cycle, each cycle ending in more advanced orienting activity. The model operationalizes internalization: material actions are progressively transformed into mental actions that orient further learning.
requirements: Teaching must be specially organized so learners pass through material, verbal, and mental levels, with orienting charts and guided formation rather than mere observation
constraints: The complete sequence of steps is a theoretical model assuming the action is perfectly new to the learner; in real learning situations steps may be abbreviated, combined, or skipped depending on prior knowledge
target_learners: adult learners acquiring substantially new content
target_learning_goals: generalization and abbreviation of learned actions
examples: Teaching experiments in handwriting, attention, geometry, elementary mathematics, history, grammar, and foreign languages from the 1950s through the 1980s
key_sources: Arievitch, I.M., & Haenen, J.P.P. (2005). Connecting Sociocultural Theory and Educational Practice: Galperin's Approach. Educational Psychologist, 40(3), 155-165. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15326985ep4003_2

article_title: Connecting Sociocultural Theory and Educational Practice: Galperin's Approach
citation: Arievitch, I.M., & Haenen, J.P.P. (2005). Connecting Sociocultural Theory and Educational Practice: Galperin's Approach. Educational Psychologist, 40(3), 155-165. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15326985ep4003_2
title: Three levels of action abstraction: material, verbal, and mental
description: Galperin classified each concrete form of an action into three basic levels of abstraction: material, verbal, and mental, each associated with a dominant way of thinking (operative, figurative, communicative, dialogical, conceptual). The article reports that "Galperin classified each concrete form of an action into three basic levels of abstraction which he called the material, the verbal, and the mental levels." Passing through all levels supports generalization (isolating essential from non-essential properties) and abbreviation (reducing operations), which together yield a fully-fledged mental action.
requirements: Each level should have its place in the teaching-learning process; several different representations of the material must be used to draw attention to essential and non-essential properties
examples: At the material level actions use hands-on manipulation or models, diagrams, and displays; at the verbal level learners think aloud; at the mental level action is performed internally

article_title: Capturing teacher priorities: Using real-world eye-tracking to investigate expert teacher priorities across two cultures
citation: McIntyre, N. A., Jarodzka, H., & Klassen, R. M. (2019). Capturing teacher priorities: Using real-world eye-tracking to investigate expert teacher priorities across two cultures. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.12.003
title: Gaze proportions as implicit micro-level indicators of explicit macro-level teacher priorities, analysed separately for attentional and communicative gaze
description: The article proposes that gaze proportions—how much a person looks at one region relative to alternatives—serve as implicit, intensive measures of teachers' enduring decision-making priorities, extending a decision-making analytic approach to educational psychology. It distinguishes attentional gaze (information-seeking, e.g., questioning) from communicative gaze (information-giving, e.g., lecturing), classifying gaze events by the speech co-occurring with them. Higher gaze proportions toward a region are interpreted as greater priority for that region.
requirements: Real-world mobile eye-tracking recordings of teaching, with simultaneous speech used to classify each gaze event as attentional or communicative
Relativized gaze proportion measures computed per participant due to uneven occurrences of gaze events across individuals
constraints: The measure accesses teachers' cognitive habits only; the article states it "does not offer an avenue for understanding teaching styles or personality as such"
Gaze proportions revealed more about teacher priorities during communicative than attentional gaze in this study
The priority measure was not triangulated with an explicit self-report measure of teacher priority
examples: 40 teachers in the UK and Hong Kong wore Tobii eye-tracking glasses during ten-minute teacher-centred episodes; gaze was coded to students, student material, teacher material, and non-instructional regions
key_sources: McIntyre, N. A., Jarodzka, H., & Klassen, R. M. (2019). Capturing teacher priorities: Using real-world eye-tracking to investigate expert teacher priorities across two cultures. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.12.003

article_title: Level of M1 GABAB predicts micro offline consolidation of motor learning during wakefulness
citation: Pasquale Cardellicchio & Sara Borgomaneri. (2025). Level of M1 GABAB predicts micro offline consolidation of motor learning during wakefulness. npj Science of Learning 10:10. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00299-1
title: GABAB-mediated disinhibition and excitation–inhibition balance as a mechanism account for rapid motor memory consolidation in M1
description: The article advances an account in which GABAB-mediated slow inhibition regulates M1 plasticity during consolidation: reduced GABAergic tone permits LTP-like Hebbian plasticity, and the excitation–inhibition balance stabilizes newly learned skills. It states that "greater GABA inhibitory tone could strongly stabilize the newly learned skill by protecting it from interference" and that inhibitory synaptic plasticity plays a key role in forming selective engrams. GABAB receptors, with their slower, prolonged action, are argued to be more significant for consolidation than fast GABAA receptors.
requirements: At-rest GABAB functioning in M1 must be measurable, here via LICI paired-pulse TMS protocols, before skill acquisition begins.
constraints: pp-TMS measures are indirect indices of GABA and glutamate levels, and MRS–TMS correspondence studies report mixed findings.
Neurophysiological measures were limited to a single session and restricted to the pre-skill-acquisition phase.
target_learners: healthy adults acquiring new motor skills
clinical populations with motor impairments such as post-stroke patients
target_learning_goals: consolidation of motor sequence skills during brief waking rest between practice blocks
examples: The study measured SICI, LICI, ICF and sICF at rest before learning and related them to micro-online and micro-offline gains during a 36-block finger-tapping task.

article_title: Optimized collusion prevention for online exams during social distancing
citation: Mengzhou Li, Lei Luo, Sujoy Sikdar, Navid Ibtehaj Nizam, Shan Gao, Hongming Shan, Melanie Kruger, Uwe Kruger, Hisham Mohamed, Lirong Xia and Ge Wang. (2021). Optimized collusion prevention for online exams during social distancing. npj Science of Learning 6:5. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00083-3
title: Grouping-based anti-collusion scheme (GAS): grouping students by competence, optimizing inter-group question overlap, and augmenting the question pool to control collusion gain below any desired level
description: The GAS is the article's core anti-collusion design for distanced online testing. It consists of three elements the article enumerates: "Grouping: Students with similar competences are grouped together to receive the same sequence of questions in an exam"; Optimization, which aggressively reduces the number of questions that can be copied between groups, even to zero; and Augmentation, enlarging the pool beyond M1 questions. It works because cyclic sequences can reduce maximum question leakage to zero when M2 - M1 + 1 >= C, grouping reduces the equivalent number of students, and similar-competence students gain little from intra-group collusion. Competences can be estimated from GPA, earlier quizzes, or a first portion of the exam via dynamic programming.
requirements: Prior knowledge of students' competences, estimated from GPA, earlier quizzes, or a first portion of the exam
constraints: The analysis is a first-order approximation of an idealized DOT scenario; intra-group collusion is facilitated because group members share the same sequence
target_learners: undergraduate students in math or fact-based courses
target_learning_goals: valid measurement of learning outcomes in remote online exams
examples: The final exam assigned M1 = 40 questions from a pool of M2 = 60 using greedy algorithms with a heuristically constructed colluding matrix P.

title: Use gamification as a complementary, optional strategy to reinforce didactic teaching rather than as a replacement for lectures
description: The article recommends integrating simple, low-cost web-based games into pharmacology curricula as a complement to lectures: using "play to complement and reinforce complex information to increase learning efficiency, rather than as a stand-alone replacement for didactic teaching." This aligns with recommendations the article cites to use game-based learning as an optional strategy and only for tedious or difficult concepts. Students' own preference for a blended approach supports this positioning.
requirements: Games centered on clear goals, incremental challenges, and immediate feedback
Free, open-access platforms so the approach works in resource-limited settings
constraints: Not beneficial for all learners; impact may depend on personality traits, and excessive game elements can overload cognitive resources beyond an optimal point per the moderate-enjoyment hypothesis
target_learners: Medical students, particularly Generation Z learners and those from engineering backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Engagement and motivation in traditionally lecture-based courses
examples: Weekly voluntary games in a 4-week pharmacology course, with lecture slides available to all students and games optional for gamers

title: Use gamification as a complement to routine teaching rather than a replacement in medical embryology education
description: The article frames gamification as an addition to existing instruction: the gamification cohort "were taught using the same routine methods supplemented by a gamification-based platform." Because that combined condition scored significantly higher on the final exam than routine instruction alone, the authors conclude that the study "supports the integration of gamification as an effective educational strategy to innovate medical curricula and enhance student learning experiences."

citation: Smith Christopher J. MD, Rohlfsen Cory MD, Wardian Jana PhD, MSW, Sahak Khalid MD. (2024). Teaching Procedural Skills: Integrating Educational Theory Into Practice. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11476
title: Gagne's nine-step model of instructional design applied to teaching procedural skills
description: Gagne's model derives from information processing theory, which "tries to explain how information is encoded into memory." It "considers the internal and external conditions of learning to create a practical, stepwise series of instructional events" comprising nine steps: gaining attention, informing learners of objectives, stimulating recall of prior learning, presenting new material, providing learning guidance, learner performance of the procedure, providing feedback, assessing performance, and enhancing retention and transfer. The workshop adopted this model as its organizing instructional framework.
requirements: Instruction proceeds through the nine stepwise instructional events in sequence
examples: The workshop presented Gagne's model step-by-step and had participants apply it in small groups to create a handwashing curriculum
